As a result, five single-point mutants (Y21F, M22I, N91S, N121I, and L135I) exhibited significantly enhanced catalytic activities relative to the wild-type enzyme (Fig. 2a). Structural analysis indicated that these mutations strengthened interactions between catalytic pocket residues and the substrate, thereby contributing to improved catalytic efficiency (Fig. 2e). Overall, the identification of these key residues provides a rational basis for engineering GgPTR1 with enhanced catalytic performance.

论文原文 | Prenyltransferases (PTs) catalyze the transfer of prenyl groups from prenyl donors to suitable acceptor molecules, resulting in prenylated products. Based on transcriptome annotation and sequence similarity analysis, four full-length candidate genes were identified and designated as GgPT1 to GgPT4 (Table S5). Transcriptome expression analysis revealed that GgPT1, GgPT2, and GgPT4 were expressed in the roots, while GgPT3 exhibited high expression in leaves (Fig. S9). Phylogenetic analysis showed that GgPT1, GgPT2 and GgPT4 clustered with PcM4DT from Psoralea corylifolia L. (Fig. S10), a prenyltransferase previously reported to transfer DMAPP to the C 4′ position of the substrate (-)-medicarpin (He et al., 2018). Conserved domain analysis revealed that the GgPT1, GgPT2 and GgPT4 belong to the PT_UbiA superfamily (PLN02878, Fig. S11).
